speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AWAKD OF VICTORIA CROSS TO MAJOR JOHN KEEFER MAHONY OF THE WESTMINSTER REGIMENT (MOTOR)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 6 I had the privilege of submitting to the house the names of almost five hundred members of the Canadian Army who had been awarded honours for deeds of gallantry in this war. With the unanimous permission of the house, these names were given a permanent record on Hansard. Among the names were two recipients of the Victoria Cross, Lieutenant-Colonel Cecil Merritt and Major Paul Triquet.
A few hours ago there was announced concurrently in the United Kingdom and in Canada that another officer of the Canadian Army has been awarded this highest honour for gallantry which can be conferred on a member of the armed forces by His Majesty the King. The recipient is Major John Keefer Mahony of New Westminster, British Columbia. His regiment is the Westminster Regiment (Motor). The award to Major Mahony is for great gallantry while leading his company in establishing and holding an important bridgehead across the river Melfa in Italy.
The citation appears in a special issue of the Canada Gazette published to-day, and I am sure the house would want it recorded in Hansard. The citation reads:
The King has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the Victoria Cross to: Major John Keefer Mahony,
The Westminster Regiment (Motor).
On the 24th May, 1944, a company of the Westminster Regiment (Motor) under the command of Major Mahony was ordered to establish the initial bridgehead across the river Melfa. The enemy still had strong forces of tanks, self-propelled guns and infantry holding defensive positions on the east side of the river. Despite this, Major Mahony personally led his company down to and across the river, being with the leading section.
Although the crossing was made in full view of and under heavy fire from enemy machine gun posts on the right rear and left front, he personally directed each section into its proper position on the west bank with the greatest coolness and confidence. The crossing was made and a small bridgehead was established on ground where it was only possible to dig shallow weapon pits. From 15.30 hours the company maintained itself in the face of enemy fire and attack until 20.30 hours when the remaining companies and supporting weapons were able to cross the river and reinforce them. The bridgehead was enclosed on three sides by an 88 mm. self-propelled gun four hundred and fifty yards to the right, a battery of four 2 cm.

Major Mahoney-Award oj Victoria Cross
anti-aircraft guns one hundred yards to the left, a spandau one hundred yards to the left of it, to the left of the spandau a second 88 mm. self-propelled gun and approximately a company of infantry with mortars and machine guns on the left of the 88 mm. From all these weapons Major Mahony'e company -was constantly under fire until it eventually succeeded in knocking out the self-propelled equipment and the infantry on the left flank.
Shortly after the bridgehead had been established the enemy counter-attacked with infantry supported iby "tanks and self-propelled guns. The counter-attack was beaten off by the company with its piats, 2-inch mortars and number 36 grenades, due to the skill with which Major Mahony had organized his defences.
With absolute fearlessness and disregard for his own safety, Major Mahony personally directed the fire of his piats throughout this action encouraging and exhorting his men. By this time the company strength had been reduced by sixty men, and all buit one of the platoon officers had been wounded. Scarcely an hour later enemy tanks formed up about five hundred yards in front of the bridgehead and in company with about a company of infantry launched a second counter-attack. Major Mahony, determined to hold the position at all costs, went from section to section with words of encouragement personally directing fire of mortars and other weapons. At one stage a section was pinned down in the open by accurate and intense machine gun fire. Major Mahony crawled forward to their position and by throwing number 77 smoke grenades, succeeded in extricating the section from its position with the loss of only one man. This counter-attack was finally beaten off with the destruction of three enemy self-propelled guns and one panther tank.
Early in the action Major Mahony was wounded in the head and twice in the leg, but he refused medical aid and continued to direct the defence of the bridgehead despite the fact that movement of any kind caused him extreme pain. It was only when the remaining companies of the regiment had crossed the river to support him that he allowed his wounds to be dressed and even then refused to be evacuated, staying instead with his company.
The forming and holding of a bridgehead across the river was vital to the whole Canadian corps action, and failure would have meant delay, a repetition of the attack, probably involving heavy losses in men, material and time and would 'have given the enemy a breathing space which might have broken the impetus of the corps' advance. Major Mahony, knowing this, never allowed the thought of failure or withdrawal to enter his mind and infused his spirit and determination into all his men. At the first sign of hesitation or faltering Major Mahony was there to encourage by his own example those who were feeling the strain of battle. The enemy perceived that this officer was the soul of the defence and consequently fired at him constantly with all weapons, from rifle to 88 mm. guns. Major Mahony completely ignored the enemy fire and with great courage and absolute disregard for personal danger commanded his company with such great confidence, energy and skill, that the enemy's efforts to destroy the bridgehead were all defeated.
The great courage shown by Major Mahony in this action will forever be an inspiration to his regiment and to the Canadian army.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that the house and the country will join very heartily in sincere congratulations to Major Mahony and to his family and to his regiment upon this worthy recognition of his superb soldierliness.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AWAKD OF VICTORIA CROSS TO MAJOR JOHN KEEFER MAHONY OF THE WESTMINSTER REGIMENT (MOTOR)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on an occasion such as this a word of comment might properly be added to the congratulations which have been so eloquently paid to Major Mahony of the Westminster regiment. I am sure it is a matter of satisfaction and gratification to the province of British Columbia that two out of three of the Victoria Crosses which have been awarded to Canadians in this war have been awarded to men from the great coastal province. I would like to add the congratulations of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition to those which have been extended by the minister to Major Mahony and to his family and regiment.

subtopic: AWAKD OF VICTORIA CROSS TO MAJOR JOHN KEEFER MAHONY OF THE WESTMINSTER REGIMENT (MOTOR)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house may I rise on this occasion to pay homage to one of Canada's great fighting men, Major John Keefer Mahony? The story of his gallent service has just been made public. Major Mahony has brought honour not only to New Westminster and British Columbia, but to all of Canada as well.
Since war started three gallant Canadian soldiers have been awarded the Victoria Cross: Lieutenant Colonel Merritt, of Vancouver; Major Paul Triquet, of Quebec, and now Major Mahony of New Westminster. It is not mere chance, Mr. Speaker, that two of Canada's Victoria Crosses have been won by men from British Columbia, and to us in New Westminster Major Mahony's achievement comes as a proud inspiration.
May I remind the house that it was a New Westminster company which was led by Major Mahony in the attack and victory obtained at the bridgehead; and so New Westminster shares a deep satisfaction in the deeds of Major Mahony and his valiant men. To gain a vital objective is a great thing; to hold on to that objective is still greater.
The achievement of Major Mahony and the men of the Westminster regiment should make those of us who remain in Canad&^more determined than ever to back up and support to the utmost of our strength and ability those who are fighting our battles overseas.
Briefly, I should like also to join with the people of New Westminster in congratulating

Major Mahony's family, and likewise the families of the men who fought with him and made his achievement possible. In acclaiming and recording the heroic deeds of the Westminster regiment we should not forget to sympathize with the relatives of those who fell in the battle, and likewise to wish the wounded a speedy recovery.

speechtext:
Will the Prime Minister take the necessary steps to make full inquiries through the protecting power into a report carried in to-day's edition, of the Globe and Mail written by Ralph Allen and' datelined "With the Canadians in France, July 11". A copy of this report I have already given the Prime Minister, but in order that the house may be aware of the subject matter of the report I shall read the first paragraph of it:
Two Canadians and "several" American prisoners of war who refused to work for the German war machine were killed by their guards at Stalag IIB near Hammeretein last February, .a repatriated French prisoner who was in the camp at the time of the killings said there to-day. The allied soldiers, all new arrivals from Italy, were shot in their beds when they refused to report for labour details, the French soldier asserted. A number of others, he said, were executed at various times by the staff of the same camp for trying to escape.
Anyone seeking to build a larger case around recent disclosures of the massacre of allied airmen in Germany could find plenty of evidence in Caen.
I should just like to make this remark, if I may, to the Prime Minister and to the government before the Prime Minister answers my question. AVhen one couples such a reported incident with the cold-blooded murder of Canadian and British airmen about which the Prime Minister spoke a couple of weeks ago, it makes one's blood boil and call loudly for the kind of punishment that these murderous vandals so richly deserve.

What is the minister's conclusion? We are widening out the scope of the aid given to taxpayers to include not only the direct progenitors and descendants of the taxpayer but also their collaterals and collaterals-in-law. How much demand has there been for this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
During the last two or three years in particular a good many representations have been received that an allowance should be made, as my hon. friend indicated last night, particularly in the case of the mother-in-law. The position under the law is that in respect of blood relations, that is to say, son, daughter, mother, father and grandparents, if they are wholly dependent upon the taxpayer, the taxpayer may claim the tax deduction set out in rule 3 of the first chedule of the act. If the son of the taxpayer were wholly dependent upon his father for support the taxpayer could claim a deduction from his tax with respect to that son, but if, on the other hand, the taxpayer were required to maintain his daughter-in-law, as is frequently the case, he could not claim a deduction.

Similarly if a man were called upon to support his own mother, who was completely dependent on him, he could claim a tax deduction, but on the other hand if he were required, as often happens, to support his wife's mother he could not claim a tax deduction. I am advised that in certain jurisdictions-I know it is the case in my own province of Quebec- there is a legal obligation on a man to support his in-laws under certain circumstances. The primary obligation rests on the blood relation, but if the blood relation is unable to give his support, or if there is no blood relation, there is a legal obligation on the in-law to support his wife's mother. It was felt after a good deal of consideration that, whatever the legal position might be, it was certainly equitable that a man who could claim a tax credit for supporting his son should be entitled to claim a similar credit for supporting his daughter-inlaw. So that the effect of the proposed amendment is to extend the tax credit not only to the blood relations but to the in-laws, though not to the collaterals, of course, as my hon. friend suggested.

I have never had any objection to extending this concession to the parents-in-law or to the grandparents-in-law, because presumably they may be in really dependent circumstances in a given case and they must be taken care of, although in the common law provinces there is no legal obligation I believe at all. But the extension of this alleviation to the collaterals is of course another matter. I wonder if there has been much demand for this. I understand that there was a very substantial demand to extend it to the parents-in-law and grandparents-in-law, but how much demand was there for extending it to sisters-in-law, brothers-in-law, sons-in-law and daughters-in-law? Has any estimate been made of the number involved and of the cost to the treasury?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not know that there has been any great demand on behalf of the other classes to which my hon. friend referred. On the other hand it was felt that in extending this to the mother-in-law, for instance, it was logical to extend it to the other in-laws. Let me give an illustration. Take the case of a man who is married and goes overseas and is killed. I suggest that in a great many cases the father of that boy would feel morally responsible at any rate to support his daughter-in-law.

I think the nation ought to support her.

4.	That the deduction in respect of unusual medical expenses be extended to include such expenses incurred outside of Canada.

On this item,, I desire to make a representation to the administration in connection with the amount of deduction for medical expenses which is permitted at the present time. My understanding is that where the medical expenses are in excess of five per cent of the taxable income, so much as is in that excess may de deducted provided the total amount does not exceed $600, plus an additional sum of $100 for each dependent, provided also that the amount which is allowed for dependents does not exceed $400. In many cases people to-day are incurring heavy medical expenses over and above the $600 limit which is provided1 by this legislation If the principle is a correct one, that over and above the five per cent some relief should be given-and I assume that that relief was allowed in the first place because of the present high rate of income tax-the ceiling on these unusual medical expenses should be lifted, because in some cases of which I have personal knowledge men have incurred considerably more expenses than the $600, and find themselves in straitened circumstances.
Take for example the case of a man whose wife has become an invalid, or whose dependent is dying, and the time which elapses between invalidity and death is considerable, say months. During the course of that time doctors' and hospital bills are heavy; frequently trips have to be taken to other centres, particularly if the afflicted person happens to be living in an out-of-the-way place. Under such circumstances the expenses in many cases exceed the limit allowed by the law.	i
This matter, I understand, has been taken Up with the department; representations have been made to it, and the replies which have been received are that it is a matter which will have to be dealt with by parliament, that the department itself has no jurisdiction to create any extension.
In addition, we find men in receipt of what may be termed a reasonable income, but with no capital ahead of them, going very heavily into debt to provide for these unusual medical expenses, and then, because of the continuation in after years of the heavy rate of -taxation on their incomes, they are never able to get out of that debt.
In addition to considering seriously the raising of the ceiling, the administration should include the services of doctors, nurses and dentists and should also provide for drugs and medical necessities which are prescribed by the doctor. We might run into a great deal of difficulty because people might take advantage of this exemption if we allowed for every kind of expenditure, but certainly if it were confined to the type certified by the doctor
Income War Tax

attending the case, I suggest that we could reasonably add such, expenses to the amount permitted at the present time. Actually what happens now is this. The doctor's fee and the hospital bill are allowed but no incidentals in the form of medicine and X-rays and matters of that sort are permitted. If a person lives in an outlying district in Saskatchewan, say, and has to go to Winnipeg or Saskatoon for treatment, he or she is not allowed anything to take care of travelling expenses or the extra money spent in going to that centre to receive badly required services. I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that the whole matter be reviewed in the light of the experience which has been gained since the exemption was included in the Income Tax Act.

I endorse what the hon. member for Saskatoon City has said. There is no necessity for repeating it except to suggest that this particular question requires a general overhauling. The only thing that is classified as medical expenses under the present regulations is what is purchased directly from the medical authorities. All the expenses outlined by the hon. member for Saskatoon City are incidental to persons getting to a centre where medical assistance can be provided. There are many other considerations also that must be taken into account. Suppose a man has an artificial leg. In the interests of his health the doctor orders him to have that leg changed, and he is obliged to spend $250 or $300 replacing it. That is a medical expenditure, but to-day it is not allowed for taxation purposes. Let me give another illustration which I have brought to the attention of the department on several occasions. A woman has an ear condition and her doctor advises her to purchase appliances costing $200. That is an order from her medical doctor, but there is no allowance for taxation purposes for a purchase of that kind. If we are going to do anything about this I think we must go the whole way or not bother with it at all.
The arrangement as applied to the lower income groups is far from satisfactory. Take a man with a $1,500 income. He is allowed to deduct if the medical expenses are in excess of five per cent of the total income. Five per cent is $75, so that he is allowed only in excess of $75, and then it is only for something that is purchased directly from the medical fraternity. I am far from satisfied with that provision, and I could elaborate on the disabilities that arise from it. It should be overhauled and made all-inclusive, or eliminated altogether. I do not think it serves much purpose in its present form. I am not

so much concerned about the man who can undertake a $1,500 expenditure to go to the United States, because a person with such an income is able to take care of his expenses and the hardship is not so great. But if this is designed to assist those in the lower income groups, then I repeat, it requires overhauling.

Considering the item
of unusual medical expenses, I would refer particularly to amputation cases. The section makes allowance only for unusual medical expenses if the payment is made to any qualified practitioner, and so on, and to one fulltime attendant upon the taxpayer in certain circumstances. As regards amputation cases, there is no provision for the purchase of an artificial limb or limbs required. It seems to put an unnecessary burden on this particular section of our population, a burden that should not be imposed on them. I have personal knowledge of one particular case. A married man without any dependent children has a salary of $1,500. He has two artificial legs and is required this year to have new limbs or he must cease working. He simply cannot carry on without them. The estimated cost of the equipment is $500, but there is not that amount of money available from his salary after he pays ordinary living expenses. If he does not buy these artificial limbs he cannot work. This and similar cases represent a genuine hardship, and I would ask the parliamentary assistant to consider widening the resolution with regard to this group of persons.

I wish to say a word in
support of the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon City and the hon. member for Cape Breton South regarding this term, "medical expenses." I think the wrong impression may be given, that the doctor gets all this money. As a matter of fact his bill is very often the small end of the stick. If a person is seriously ill he may require special nurses, and under the present regulations one nurse is not enough because they work an eight-hour day and therefore it is necessary to have three nurses. Three nurses at $7 a day each means $21. There are a number of other incidentals such as those mentioned by my hon. friends. I suggest therefore that this should be more specific, and should cover a wider territory than is indicated by the term "medical expenses."

It was never intended that the income tax act should serve as a health insurance or a sickness insurance measure. Because the rates of taxation were put up very steeply in 1941 it was felt that in the case of unusual, exceptional medical expenses some measure of relief should be given to the taxpayer. Under ordinary circumstances a good many men who run into unforeseen and heavy medical taxes have either to dip into their capital, if they have any, or try to borrow money if they have none. It was not felt that the income tax act could be used as a vehicle to provide for universal health or sickness insurance. This was an alleviating measure to give some relief in exceptional circumstances; therefore I cannot agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that it should be wholly revised in order to take care of every possible case. Perhaps it does not go far enough, but I am not prepared to say that. Perhaps there should be some raising of the ceiling as suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon, although my view is it is undesirable under existing circumstances. When they become ill their earning power ceases and they have to have some consideration. The question is how far it should go. Personally I am willing to see the limit raised and relief given; but that was not the purpose for which I rose to speak. I want to talk about the concession contained in resolution 4, as follows:
That the allowance in respect of unusual medical expenses be extended to include such expenses incurred outside of Canada.
I never could understand why, if it was a sound principle to grant to a taxpayer an allowance for unusual or usual medical expenses, there was a geographical limitation to its application. Take the case of people who live along the border near Boston or New York. In exceptional surgical cases in my part of the country it has been the usual practice to send patients not only to Montreal but to certain clinics in Boston and in the city of New York. Up to the present time there has been no allowance made to a Canadian taxpayer. Apparently the department has had a change of heart, and I am going to ask that they make it retroactive. It ought to have been done from the beginning. If the principle is good now, it was good last year, and those who have to pay unusual expenses should be given some consideration in the circumstances I have mentioned.
I am going to give a concrete case. I suppose concrete cases are those that come to our minds and impress themselves upon our memory. A lady from Charlottetown visited her brother who was a physician in New York. She was suddenly taken ill and had to undergo an intricate and expensive operation which cost her husband a good deal of money. While she was convalescent her husband, after a good deal of difficulty, was able to get enough money from the foreign exchange control board to go across the line to see her. I am not complaining about that, because he should have been able to get the exchange very easily in

the circumstances if he had gone about it in the right way. The banker, I think, could have given him the money very quickly, but there was some delay. Mr. COTE The department has admitted the principle in the case of two or more groups of irregular practitioners, generally known as such; though without any specific standing in the whole country they may be recognized in one or two provinces, and that is all. The optometrists are now considered a

May I on this clause make a plea once more for the simplification of income tax returns?
This is a matter which is very seriously bothering a very great number of income tax payers. It does not interest them in the least that an official of the income tax division says it is now quite a simple matter, that all they need is a pencil, and they have to sit down and answer some questions. That is not the way the public see it.
The minister referred to this in passing in his speech at the end of the debate, and drew attention to the fact that the complexity which

Income War Tax
has crept into the forms is largely due to the desire oi the minister to give as much equity to the taxpayer as he can. But that really does not give any hope for a further simplification. The fact that the compulsory savings are no longer to be followed, he considers, is going to be of very great assistance in this regard. Although it is going to help, I have no doubt, it comes near the end of the list of questions which have to be answered and statements which have to be made, and it does not seem to me that it will affect in simplification the whole questionnaire which each taxpayer has to answer.
Various incidents have been brought to the attention of members, and I have taken several of them up with the Minister of National Revenue. Let me cite one. In the city of Vernon an accountant, to assist in the difficulty of shortage of forms, handed some of his T-l forms to the postmaster on the understanding that another supply of these forms was on the way from Vancouver and he would have his forms replaced. These forms arrived on April 29, by which time the accountant had collected the facts and figures in regard to the cases of his clients and it was a physical impossibility for him to fill in the returns on these forms and get them in to satisfy the due date and avoid the penalty. He took the matter up in the form of a letter, I believe, to the minister. He received a reply that the penalty was mandatory and there would be no way of assisting him. If his facts are correct, this was a matter that was in no way either his fault or that of his clients. I remember, in discussing the matter with the Minister of National Revenue, he drew my attention to the fact that if in such a case the taxpayer would put in an interim return and, I presume, accompany it with a partial payment it would reduce his liability for penalty at least by that amount. But I wonder whether the taxpaying public are aware of the fact that they can avoid a portion of the penalty by filling in a partial return; or are the public aware that a letter to the department under these circumstances would suffice so far as the full penalty is concerned. That is one type of trouble which these accountants have to meet.
There is another one that came to my attention from another accountant who had considerable difficulty in completing the returns necessary for his clients and endeavouring to avoid the penalty. He makes the point that the taxpayer, if he falls short in what he ought to do, is mulcted in a penalty, but the taxpayer who has sent in by mistake too large a sum of money for his needs may have that amount returned to him one year
or two or three years after that. He argues that the government therefore has the use of that money of the taxpayer without paying interest, and he is of the opinion that this is just one of the instances in which the taxpayer is out of luck. He considers that it is not fair to those who may be endeavouring to fulfil the requirements of the income tax act.
I drew this matter also to the attention of the department and in the accountant's subsequent letter to me he says:
I note that he does not say anything about how long it takes his department to prepare the forms from the closing of the session until they are available to the public. If he would speed up the distribution of the new forms, lots of forms could be filed sooner.
I quite agree, as was pointed out to me by the minister, that in many of these cases the taxpayer is at fault by delaying the matter too long, and in many cases he delays it too long because he is not able to understand what is required of him, and then the accountant has the information from many clients lying on his desk and he cannot get the things filled up in time. He calls attention also to the fact that he reads in the newspapers that the national selective service does not consider that office help is a necessity and he has to do what he can to fill in these many forms. I continue with the letter:
If there was any truth to his statement as *to filing of these returns, I wonder why the department is still requesting information on 1938, 1939 and 1940 returns. A few 1942 assessments are trickling in, but any number of taxpayers have not yet received their 1941 assessment. I myself have received nothing since 1940. Possibly he could explain why there are no explanations attached to the additional assessments sent out on T-l general returns. No one will pay on something he does not understand, and this only means a letter back to the department for an explanation when the assessor has to look it up and prepare a reconciliation, an unwarranted waste of time for the assessor, a stenographer and the accountant who has the returns in hand and finds it necessary to request further information. According to the papers, the government officials have declared office help non-essential, so how do they expect to have the forms made out in time? Does the department intend to penalize the taxpayers the full five per cent of their assessments for late filing where they, the department, have had excess payments in hand for two and three years?
That is an amplification of the remark I made just now. I replied to the accountant and had a subsequent letter from him from Which I quote a couple of sentences:
I have just returned from Vancouver, where I spent the best pant of three days at the income tax department on various matters. While there I was advised that the 1943 returns of individuals-business returns-were
Income War Tax

not even filed, which was 'borne out by files produced. Apparently very few 1942 business forms have been assessed and the assessors appear loath to assess any particular one when asked, preferring to have them come in rotation.
With regard to the inability of the public to follow the requirements of the forms, it does not apply only to the general public, but is strikingly so in the case of agricultural returns. I have always been of the opinion that one of the reasons why so few farmers come into the income tax paying class, according to the statistics, is the fact that as they do not keep the books which a firm keeps they find it extremely difficult to supply the answers demanded of them in the questionnaire and make them fit in with the return they should put in.
I make my plea for further consideration of this difficulty, so that simplification may be arrived at which in the long run will be of great assistance to the minister in getting in returns for income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I have not the letter that
the hon. member has been reading from, so that I may find it difficult to deal with all the points that he has raised. First of all, he dealt with the simplification of the tax forms. As the Minister of Finance has said, we can do little to simplify the forms further while our tax structure remains as it is. The department, in preparing the form, has to make provision for the numerous allowances made to ease the burden on the taxpayer, and every new form of relief granted the taxpayer must be included on the form; otherwise the taxpayer himself may not have the knowledge that he is entitled to such relief. That was brought to my attention the other day, when it was pointed out that we had not mentioned on the form that alimony payers were entitled to some relief. We have extended the relief this year granted to those who pay alimony, and I presume that this further provision will have to be added to the form. This year, while we are removing the compulsory savings feature, it remains for half the year. I conclude from that that it will also have to be provided for on the form for the coming year. That is the difficulty of the income tax department. We have had representations made to us-I think I have mentioned this before- that agricultural returns should be simplified. We had a meeting of agricultural representatives, representatives of the farm journals, the agricultural societies, the Department of Agriculture. They conferred for quite a considerable time in order to devise a simplified form that would be satisfactory to the farmer. As a result of their labours they brought in a 
form that was considerably more complicated than the one our own experts had already produced. That shows the difficulty. It is easy to criticize, but it is not easy to devise a form that contains all the information that must be included in it.
We now come to the question of the filing of the returns. Now that the tax structure has become more complicated, and there are a great many more taxpayers than in former years, many people have adopted the policy of going to an accountant to have their tax returns prepared and filed. The result has been that particularly just at the closing date for the filing of the returns the accountants find themselves flooded with work. They have far more clients coming in than they can deal with, and we get emergency calls saying, "For heaven's sake extend the time for filing returns." If that is done one year it would be expected every year. While we have endeavoured to meet the public as far as possible, and particularly in times when there have been changes in the tax structure and we have been late in preparing the new tax form, we cannot start the practice of setting a date for the filing of returns, and then extending the date when that date is reached. Where there is reasonable excuse for not having all the details of the tax return completed we have authorized the taxpayer to file an incomplete return which will act as a substitute for the final return when the full information is available. That has been done in order to avoid the incurring of a penalty through causes over which the employee may have no control.
Is that generally known?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I do not think it is generally known, and it is not the general practice. We do not extend that privilege to all taxpayers so that they may simply file a blank return and complete one at their leisure. There must be some reasonable excuse or a valid reason for not having the completed return filed when it is due.
Therefore the taxpayer must first of all get in touch with the district inspector and get the permission.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Give reasons.
Would a letter do?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
No; we must file a form.
It has been mentioned that when we assess the taxpayer we do not always give details of the amendments that have been made in his assessment. We do give details where a change is substantial, but we realize that with the limited staff we have to-day in many cases

Income War Tax
details are not required if the change in the assessment is a dollar or two. If it is only a small amount we make the change in the assessment notice and we do not give details unless the taxpayer asks for them.
They are simply informed that they owe so many more dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
How many more dollars have been added to the income. If they want full details they are supplied.
Reference has been made to the fact that the income tax department is behind in assessing of the returns. I am sorry to say that that is true, and although we are doing everything we can to keep up to date, the very large increase in the number of taxpayers-it has increased from 200,000 to roughly 2,000,000- has created a tremendous load on the income tax department. At the same time we have not been able to secure the staffs that we require. It is necessary to secure qualified or experienced accountants, and unless we can get experienced accountants we cannot keep up with the assessing. No matter how many stenographers or clerks we have they are not able to go ahead with the assessing of the returns until they have been dealt with by the assessors; consequently we have had difficulty with regard to personnel. In many districts we have had difficulty in getting income tax premises. In some centres where we have district officers we have the greatest difficulty in securing space, and members of the staff are so crowded that they can scarcely move. These are some of the difficulties with which we have been contending, and that is the reason why practically all of our offices have fallen behind in the assessing of returns. They are certainly making every effort to pick up ground that has been lost, and as men, particularly qualified accountants, are released from the armed forces we are making every effort to secure them on our staffs so that the work in each district office can be proceeded with as rapidly as possible.
Would the minister deal with the question of no interest being paid on the amount of money the taxpayer has overpaid the government, whereas a penalty is exacted if he pays too little?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I understand that at one time-I do not know whether or not they still do it-the United States used to pay interest on overpayments of tax.
Six per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Yes, I think that was the rate. That became a very valuable form of investment, and there was nothing to prevent
a man from overpaying a tax by any considerable amount that he had available, and drawing six per cent on it. From that point of view it has not seemed to be a very wise measure. If we were keeping our work up to date, as we normally do, it would not take as long to make assessments and the taxpayer would not be without the use of his money for long periods.

I should like to urge upon the minister the necessity of seeing that the income tax forms are more simplified, particularly in regard to agriculture. At the back of the blue sheet which is attached to the farmer's return there is a paragraph which reads:
Produce raised on farm and consumed in the farm home.
The farmer is asked to estimate the amount that he takes from his farm to be consumed by his family. Another paragraph reads:
Produce used from "family garden" and small sums usually termed "pin-money" obtained by the wife, sons or daughters, by their own effort, need not be taken into account.
The other form goes on to say that the vegetable garden does not count. I have a particular case in my own riding where a family of four persons estimated that they had consumed $90 worth of produce from their farm in 1942. After making their income tax return to the district office they found themselves in this position. They were charged $500 for the produce that they had consumed from the farm, or a difference of $410. The point I should like to emphasize is this: Why ask the farmer to estimate the amount he has consumed from his farm if there is to be an arbitrary amount set? Why not tell him in the first place that he is to be charged $125 per person for the vegetables and the milk or whatever is consumed from the farm? If that is done he will know immediately. But to ask a man to estimate the amount he takes off his farm and consumes in his own household; then put an arbitrary amount, as in this case. $410 more, and then send an assessment to him and charge him interest at the rate of five per cent is not fair to any farmer, nor do I think is it fair to any person in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member think the farmer made a fair assessment?

I certainly do, and I have a list in my hand showing what he used off his farm. In the first place, he does not make butter in his own home; he purchased all of it. He does not kill his own meat; he purchased all of it. He keeps seven or eight hundred hens, and has for consumption in his own home all the eggs that are not salable.

Income War Tax
This form says that he need not estimate them at any cost. Yet in this case, the farmer did estimate that he used at least three dozen in his home every week, and put them in at the market price. He shows the amount of milk he used-two quarts a day, which I think the minister must admit is a fair amount. The form says that he shall estimate it only at the price for which he sells it wholesale. Well, when he appeared at the district income tax office and asked those in charge to make up a statement showing how he could possibly get 8500 worth of commodities for consumption in his own home, they took into account milk at twelve cents a quart, chicken at forty cents a pound, and so on all down the line.
There is certainly something definitely wrong somewhere. Either the form should be simplified, or some standard amount should be set for each and every person on the farm. There should be no attempt to make a fool out of a man by asking him to estimate what is used, and then, when he does it with perfect honesty, say to him, "You are all wrong; you are not even twenty per cent right."

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: But farmers do not all produce the same commodities. That is one difficulty.

That is true. If the farmer knew he was to be charged $100 per person or $125 per person a year for commodities he consumed he would be privileged to consume that amount if he so desired, because he would know that he would be charged with it. But in this instance, and in every instance where the farmer has to make a return, he is asked to give an estimate. Then, after he makes the estimate, and that estimate goes to the income tax office, he is reassessed, and an arbitrary amount of, I believe, $125 per person is put on.
I urge the minister to see that this form is simplified, so that men who are honest and who are endeavouring to make their returns as farmers will not be faced with this condition.

speechtext: I was just inquiring as to what consideration has been given.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Where a man has no children, do you mean?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In one of the complaints I hold in my hand it is pointed out that the man is a widower, whose wife died a short time ago, and whose establishment has been carried on. His is a fully self-contained establishment. He has had to hire a housekeeper to look after things and, in addition, he states that he is penalized, as against the single man. He finds himself in a position where he has an exemption only as a single man, instead of a position in which many people who are in the marital stage find themselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I apologize to my hon.
friend; I spoke too quickly. I assumed that the hon. member was speaking of a widower with children. In the case which he has cited, that would be a mode of life, as it were. The man has had married status and the exemptions which go with married status, but after the death of his wife, in effect he was in no different position from that of a bachelor who maintains an apartment or has a house with a housekeeper, and therefore he is given no special tax consideration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was not clear from the letter I had in my hand as to whether he had children.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If he has children he will
receive additional relief as is proposed in resolution 8.

Is that exactly fair? Many men in that category maintain homes simply because they want to have some gathering place for their children who have married and left the home. There is always that place for them. I feel that that type of man should receive some consideration under those circumstances. He does not maintain a home simply because he wants some place to live by himself; he maintains a home so that his children may gather there at times. There is a good deal of family complexion about that type of home.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would be pretty difficult to give consideration in a case like that and not give it to the old bachelor who has a lot of nephews and nieces who like to gather around him in a family circle.

There is no comparison.
The bachelor did not have those nieces and nephews; they just happened.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
With regard to the question of the simplification of forms there is one matter I should like to bring to the attention

Income War Tax

of the parliamentary assistant. This has been pointed out to me by a member of a group in a city on the west coast who have made a special effort to see what can be done to simplify the income tax form. He points out that one difficulty they have come across in their group discussions is the fact that item 17 on the income tax return asks whether or not the marital partner is in receipt of an investment income of over $660.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt
my hon. friend; but while it may not be clear from the terms of the resolution, resolution 10 deals directly with the question of whether the wife has an income in excess of $660.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The point I desire to
raise has nothing to do with the actual amount. My correspondent points out that in some circumstances there is no way by which the marital partner can ascertain the exact income of the other partner; and he thinks a justifiable complaint can be made about that question being asked. I simply draw the matter to the attention of the parliamentary assistant.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I suppose if the husband
cannot find out what his wife's income is he would have no alternative than to put in the form, "Unknown to me." I must confess that the point had never occurred to me, but it is well taken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Apropos of that, this
group which has been making a study of income tax matters held a miniature Gallup poll and found out that of those in the lower income brackets, sixty-eight per cent of the husbands did not know their wives' incomes and thirty-two per cent of the wives did not know their husbands' incomes. Of those in the higher income brackets, thirty-five per cent of the husbands did not know their wives' incomes and sixty-five per cent of the wives did not know their husbands' incomes. I only offer this as a matter of information for the parliamentary assistant. I have no recommendation to' make.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am glad to have that information.

When I referred to the widower who is keeping up a home the parliamentary assistant mentioned the bachelor, supposing a bachelor had an illegitimate child which he was keeping in his home, he would be entitled to exemption.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
He would have to have a housekeeper.
[Mr. Graydon.J

Depending on the age of
the child. Nevertheless the fact is that a bachelor with an illegitimate child in his home receives an exemption, while the widower who maintains a home because he wants it as a gathering place for his family, cannot get an exemption. I have no references to make.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Like some other hon. members, the hon. member for York South had to leave the chamber to attend the meeting of the banking and commerce committee, but he asked me if I would raise a point in connection with resolution 7. I understand that he has been in touch with the departmental officials about this and has been told that the matter is being looked into. As I understand it, the situation is this. A single person maintaining a self-contained domestic establishment and supporting therein, we will say his mother, is granted the status provided by this section only if that mother's income is less than $400. My colleague suggests that there seems to be discrimination as between that man and the married man whose wife's income does not exceed $660.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He does not get the $150 exemption if his wife's income is over $660.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The only point my colleague asked me to raise was the difference between the $400 and the $660. I do not suggest that the same allowance should be made widespread for all classes, but I think a single man maintaining his mother might be given the same status as a married man.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The language of the statute is that the dependent must be wholly dependent. I am informed by the income tax division that that is taken to mean if the income of the dependent does not exceed $400 per annum. I suppose under a strict interpretation of the law, if the mother had any income at all she would not be wholly dependent. There had to be some standard and I am advised that the $400 figure was fixed. In other words, a person may still be considered as a dependent although he has a private income of $400 a year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it that no change is contemplated?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No change is contemplated under the present resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is one question I should like to ask under this item, with reference to tax forms. I spoke about this the other night in the general budget debate. The receipts issued by the income tax branch show the amount only in figures. I cited a

Income War Tax
case which had given the department some considerable difficulty in straightening it out, and I feel that that would not have happened if the receipt had showed the amount both in figures and in words. It may be that the work involved would be too great, but it seems to me that receipts for income tax payments might well be made up in such a way as to show the amount both in figures and in words.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member, but when millions of receipts are going out, if we had some, for example, for $2,222.15 and they had to be written out on the typewriter in full, it would slow down the getting out of receipts very considerably and we would not be able to get them out as quickly as we do by simply showing the figures only on the receipts. I agree that it would be preferable to show it both ways, but with the shortage of staff I do not think it is practical to adopt that method at the present time.

How much income is a child allowed to have before it is no longer classified as a dependent, and does it make any difference whether that income forms part of the family budget or is allowed to accumulate for the child?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that the same rule is applied as is applied with respect to the mother, $400. There might be some modification in sheer infancy but, broadly speaking, that is the general rule. The child is considered as wholly dependent on the father.
Is the $400 applicable to the wife? I thought it was $660.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We are talking about
children.
It makes no difference whether the child's independent income goes into the family budget or is simply accumulated on behalf of the child?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We do not distinguish.
There are deductions allowed if the taxpayer has a child in a self-contained establishment and employs a housekeeper. He gets a tax credit of $80, plus $28, plus $150 for his married status.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is covered by resolution 8. We are still on resolutiton 7, but the two really go together.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are on resolution 7. I have called it carried.
Resolution agreed to
100-303i
8.	That, if a taxpayer maintains one of his children in a self-contained domestic establishment in which he employs a full-time housekeeper or servant, the tax credits of $80 against the graduated tax and $28 against the normal tax be allowed to 'him in respect of the child notwithstanding that he is entitled to the tax credit of $150 against the graduated tax in respect of that child.

If a man has a housekeeper he is allowed a tax credit of $150, but if he is earning a salary and his wife has an income of over $660 they are both classed as single and do not get the $150 tax credit. That does not seem quite right. I think that the man and wife should be allowed that $150.
Both of them?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Under the law as it stands and has stood for some time, if both husband and wife have an income, let us say the wife has the smaller income and that it exceeds $660, both then lose the $150 tax credit as having married, status. It may be arbitrary, but I assume that the justification for it is that the total income is so large that they should not have this special exemption. It is intended primarily for the spouse who is the entire support of his family.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
9.	That the basis of taxation under the normal tax and the tax credit against the graduated tax for a married person be limited to a married person who supports the spouse.
What does this cover?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: At present the law by definition automatically allows a. married person as such to get $150 tax exemption.
Whether he supports her or not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. The husband can obtain this $150 tax credit although he may not have been contributing a dollar to his wife's support and the wife is supported by the son. This credit of $150 for a married person will go to the person who supports the spouse.
It takes it away from the man who does not do the supporting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is it; and as you realize, under the other section, the son would get the $150.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
4S24
Income War Tax

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 10.	That individuals may reduce income for taxation purposes by the amount of gifts made in money to His Majesty in right of Canada if such gifts are made within the year when the income was received or within four months from the end thereof.
Would this language, "gifts made in money to His Majesty in right of Canada if such gifts are made within the year", cover gifts of corvettes to His Majesty's Canadian navy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; they must be gifts to the crown.
Outright cash?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Outright cash. As I indicated in answering a question by the leader of the opposition, this provision is really intended to give relief to a marginal case where the wife's income is, let- us say, 1665 a year, and as a result of having that $5 over S660 her husband has to pay an extra tax of, say $200. Under these circumstances there is no benefit to the husband and wife in having that extra- $5, and under this provision she can make a donation of $5 to the crown and the husband will then retain his exemption as a married man.
I suggest that that is a very funny formula. It is some amelioration. I suppose it is a difficult situation to meet by draftsmanship.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was an extremely difficult situation to take care of.
If I give to His Majesty in right of Canada a Red Cross ambulance, do I get the benefit of this provision?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I can illustrate it best by taking the case of a married woman who has an income of, say $1,000, and whose husband happens to have a very large earned income. As a result of the S340 of income which the wife has over the $660, her husband may have to pay a tax very substantial!}' in excess of the $340. It was felt that that was ' unfair, and) we have had a number of representations to that effect.
It is unfair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In a number of cases the wife would convert her resources into cash, leaving her without taxable income, but where her income was received under a will or trust that might not be possible. It is now provided that if the wife wishes to do so she may surrender to the crown the amount of income she receives in excess of $660, and in that case her husband will be taxed as a married person

and get the tax credit and be taxed at the rates that apply to a married person. I think this is a fair and reasonable and justifiable concession to the class of taxpayer.
And the wife would escape taxation altogether?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
She would pay roughly $300
in taxation.

I have no doubt that that is the objective, but this resolution is wider in scope than that. I put this to the minister. Let us say that I give $1,000 to His Majesty, and in the early stages of the war a good many people did donate whatever amount the army said was necessary to buy an ambulance. Under this resolution I could get a reduction in my taxation by the amount of that gift. Is that the law now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I wonder if my hon. friend would just repeat his question? I was having a word with the deputy.
I understand that the objective is to give relief to the husband and wife where the wife's income is just a little over $660.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Primarily to give relief to the husband, or to give joint relief.

It gives relief to both, or it should at all events. But the scope of this resolution is wider than that. It is not limited at all. As I read it, any individual may reduce his income for taxation purposes by the amount of the gifts he made to His Majesty in the right of Canada if the gifts "are made within the year when the income was received or within four months from the end thereof." This is new law.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.
What was the position with respect to gifts before? Was there any allowance made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They would have to be included under charitable donations and be subject to the limitation of ten per cent.
That clears my point up.

Under this wording suppose somebody makes a patriotic gift such as was suggested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury. He might give it in the form of a deduction from his capital; yet under this phraseology he would be allowed to reduce his taxable income by the amount of the gift he made in that year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is correct.

Income War Tax
That is fair enough too.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Resolution 10 represents a provision which has been drafted to take care of an anomaly which has developed in connection with the situation of a man and wife both having earned income. There is another anomaly in the case of a man and wife both having earned income which this provision does not take care of, and which I should like to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant.
I may say that we do not seem to be getting along very well this afternoon; we have made a large number of suggestions, but I am afraid our batting average is very poor.
You mean you do not get any concessions. You never do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
None of our suggestions has been accepted yet to-day. I hope we can change the rule. I realize that most of the suggestions we make one year are accepted the next year, but let us get this one this year.
Let me state the case to the parliamentary assistant in concrete form. Here is the case of a man and wife, both of them medical doctors; and the parliamentary assistant knows that medical doctors are needed in this country and should be encouraged to carry on their practice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My own doctor is in that position; his wife is a doctor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Which one do you go to?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said, my own doctor's wife is a doctor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The purpose of the provision that a married lady may have earned income of any amount-is not that the case; at least it may go over $660, anyway, without its affecting the married staus of the husband- is to encourage them to work. Now, put the two together. We need doctors. The general desire of the government is to encourage married women to work. These two things add up to this, that the government, should encourage lady doctors to practise their profession. In the case I refer to

and maybe my hon. friend's doctor's wife is in the same position-here is the situation. The wife, who is a practising physician, has, as a great many doctors have, her own clientele and receives her fees individually from her patients. Because she receives her income in that way as fees from patients and makes over $660, her husband is put on a single status, on the ground that what she receives is not wages or salary, but something else.
As I understood it, the reason for drawing the line which was established was to distinguish between earned income and unearned income, such as invested income from various sources. But take again the case of the lady doctor. If the person to whom I refer was working for a clinic, supposing the clinic consisted of only two or three doctors and the fees were paid to that clinic as such; if she were on salary, even though she received more than she gets now, that would be treated as wages or salary and her husband would be given married status.
That is true not only for married lady doctors, but for married nurses. I think I am correct in this, because I have been in touch with the Minister of National Revenue about it, and I have his letter to this effect: if a married nurse goes on to the staff of a hospital and receives a monthly salary, no matter whether it exceeds $660 a year, her husband is allowed a married status, but if the married nurse takes special cases and receives her fees individually from the patients, either in hospital or in the home-and I put in by way of parenthesis again that we need nurses and that the government is anxious to have these married nurses practise their profession wherever possible-in that case the husband is forced to take a single status if his wife makes over S660. For the life of me I cannot see the reason for the department sticking to that technicality. The letters I have seen, both those addressed to me and copies I have had of letters which have gone to people who are affected by this ruling, simply say that the fees a married lady, be she doctor or nurse, receives on special cases are fees, not wages or salary as defined by the act, and that therefore the husband cannot have a married status. But it seems to me that this business of applying a rule and sticking to the line has been carried a little too far in this case; bearing in mind that the government time and again has said that one of the things it takes into consideration in formulating tax policy is its desired ends, bearing in mind that one of the ends is to encourage doctors and nurses to practise their respective professions, I feel that this line of discrimination should not be drawn, and that we should get away from the practice the parliamentary assistant has followed thus far of only receiving our suggestions and filing them; I hope something will be done with this suggestion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
On that point, this was a piece of emergency legislation, and it was introduced because it was found that we needed women workers in the factories pretty badly and for some reason or another they were not willing to go and work-per-
Income War Tax

haps we cannot blame them-if it meant that their husbands were going to be penalized by a somewhat higher income tax; they would stop when they got to $660 a year. So that on grounds of expediency, if you will, this measure was introduced last year. Incidentally it would appear to discriminate against the lady doctor, for instance-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And the married nurse.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -and the married nurse. But my view is that we probably should not have had it in the legislation at all, on the strict ground of principle. Nevertheless we have had to put it in so as to ensure the services of these workers. I will bring the remarks of my hon. friend to the attention of the minister, but my belief is that the principle should not be extended.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is not a case of
intimidation, but I want to give the actual case in human terms of two doctors I know. The lady in question has indifferent health; it has been touch-and-go with her whether to continue in practice or not, and I am afraid that this may be the deciding factor. I do not say it is the whole cause which may lead her to discontinue her practice, but in the situation as it has been, the considerable difference which it makes to their total tax may be the deciding factor. If that is the case with the married lady doctor, I imagine there must be a good many cases similar to that so far as special nurses are concerned, because special nurses are in a little different situation from that of the lady doctor who has her office and an established practice. A special nurse might take cases or she might decide not to do so, because she would be in exactly the position described by the parliamentary assistant with respect to war workers. Once she gets up to $660 she may take the view that working will result in a loss rather than in a gain to her and her husband. She may decide that there is no point in doing it. We are dealing with human situations. The parliamentary assistant has admitted that this is a matter of expediency and I cannot see any sense in drawing the line where it has been drawn. I hone that when the parliamentary assistant takes the matter up with the minister and his officials they will give favourable consideration to my representations.

I had hoped that the parliamentary assistant, who is new to his position, would bring a fresh point of view to bear upon it and not so easily succumb to the chill atmosphere, the love of theory and of easy administration, which to my mind has
permeated both these departments for some considerable time now. There is nothing anomalous about the situation mentioned by the hon. member who spoke before me. No wife will take on work in any field, whether in home nursing, in medical practice, or in a munitions factory if it will have such an effect on the joint income of husband and wife that the family as a unit will secure no return from her efforts. That situation will obtain whether in war or in peace, and this committee is not very much concerned with the theory of taxation as suggested by the parliamentary assistant. The question is whether iwe can get goods and services produced for the Canadian people; and in my opinion, instead of being bound by some slight technicality, as the department is permitting itself to be bound at the present time, the parliamentary assistant should take a broader view. Surely he is allowing himself to succumb to a technicality. Even if the whole rule were changed a year or so ago, after insistence on the part of the opposition, being finally adopted by the administration, even if it were changed as a matter of expediency, I believe the expedient is a sound one; even though it may be against some theory of taxation, it is one .which should be embodied as a principle of taxation under the laws of the country and carried into the post-war period. Otherwise we shall find our taxation laws keeping goods and services from being produced for the Canadian people. I maintain that the taxation laws should be made for the people and not the people for the taxation laws. The thing is entirely unfair, and I am not content to have the parliamentary assistant say that he will carry our grievance to the minister and perhaps obtain some redress. I simply wish to reassert what has been previously said, that suggestions made in this house one year, or two or three years ago, have been pigeon-holed and filed by the administration, and finally they are brought out as amendments to the income tax act, but long after the necessity for them has made itself felt-and, as my hon. friend says, on the eve of an election, although I do not think that refers to this particular case. Here we have an urgent need for more nurses in the field, more lady doctors, greater production of all types and more services; and yet the government is adamant about the matter, although it merely carries out an expedient which it adopted in a previous year and which, I submit, should be put into the form of a principle applicable throughout our taxation in Canada, in war time as well as in peace.

Income War Tax
What is the objection to going the whole way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We want more workers in the plants. I suppose, if there are not enough nurses or lady doctors we may have to add additional financial inducements to get them, but somebody else will have to pay the taxes that they do not pay.

Not at all. That is where the parliamentary assistant is wrong. He says that somebody else will have to pay the taxes; nothing of the sort. The money will not be earned because the goods will not be produced and the services will not be rendered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend takes a lower view of the professional classes than I do.

I have the floor for the moment. These goods will not be produced, nor will the services be rendered because it will not be worth a person's while. It is no use advancing theories about morals and practicality. People must have some inducement. The minister himself said so. Why does he remove the compulsory savings? It is not to remove taxation at all; the object is that people shall have money. And they must have it in their pockets. That is the only effect which the removal of the compulsory savings provision will have so far as the people are concerned. In this case no one will pay the tax, because the value of these goods and services will not be created and therefore there will be no tax and no increase in the standard of living for the people. It is this sort of thinking that keeps the country behind, and it is high time that the income tax department and those who are supposed to be dictating the laws of the country in that regard, or presenting them to us for our consideration, decided to listen to what members of parliament have to say, speaking from their experience.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am all for lower taxes, but I think it is a little too early to go at it too hard.

I am asking the parliamentary assistant a question. If these people do not work, what will happen? We had it from my hon. friend that this is a definite question, from a practical case which he brought before the committee, of a nurse who, if her bus-band is reduced to single tax status, will not find it worth while. People do not work without making some sacrifice, and they must be given a reward for working in war time just as well as in peace time. The parliamentary assistant said that someone else will pay the taxes. 'If these people do not work, for the reason that there is no incentive for them to work by reason of the effect which this taxation will have, is somebody else going to pay the extra taxes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. Someone else is going to pay the taxes. We know what our budget will be. I do not believe that a concession of $150 to a married woman, or two per cent in the tax rate, will prevent any self-respecting doctor or self-respecting nurse from working under existing conditions when the country needs their services. My hon. friend may think so, but I do not.
The parliamentary assistant does not understand much about life.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think I understand as much as my hon. friend does.

If a lady doctor or a lady nurse goes out she will have to get someone to look after the house. There are always expenses that must be incurred in earning income. I know situations where people have had to get someone else to look after the children. A woman may have left her profession for a few years and now decides to answer the call for nurses or doctors, but if there is absolutely no monetary incentive for her to do so she may not feel it worth while. I do not see what objection there is from the point of view of administration.

Strange as it may seem to the parliamentary assistant, human nature is very much as suggested by my colleague. Not many weeks ago I had an illustration of a lady residing in this city, who was a competent stenographer and who had an opportunity to take a position with the wartime prices and trade board, shall I say-M have forgotten exactly. She was in receipt of a substantial dependents' allowance because of the service of her son. She was in a quandary to know whether she should take the job and lose the dependents' allowance or not. I tried to figure it out mathematically to show that she would be better off, but she said, "What about the taxes I have to pay if I take the job? I can sit back quietly and live on the dependents' allowance, or I can work eight hours a day for the government and have them take from me so much out of my pay cheque-so much deduction for this, so much for deduction for war saving certificates, and what-not." She
Income War Tax

said, "I had better be an idle fool." I tried to controvert that frame of mind. It was a frame of mind. I am not sure that I was successful. Therefore there is something in what the hon. member for Rosedale has said. The parliamentary assistant cannot just toss it off by saying that people will be patriotic. People want an incentive. I think he will recognize that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, I recognize that. My contention is that the incentive is not completely removed.

I am sorry that I
missed a part of the discussion. Do I understand that resolution 10 has a provision whereby an individual may make a gift of a small sum to the government in order to avoid paying a larger sum?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member's colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, is, I think, fully aware of the purpose of this resolution. It is to enable a wife, which is a typical case, to make a gift to the crown of the amount of income she has in excess of $660 in order to prevent her husband from losing the benefit of the tax rates applicable to a married person. In other words, it may happen that a wife whose income happens to run over $660, say $665, may involve her husband in the payment of some $150 or $200 additional tax. It was felt that was unfair. The wife, of course, could obviously correct that by selling something or by reducing her income to $660. It was felt that it was unreasonable to expect that sort of thing to be done.
Is there anything to prevent a taxpayer from making a small donation to the government that would get him in a lower income bracket?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
But I assume he would
derive no benefit from that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to call the
parliamentary assistant's attention to the language he just used in referring to what is now the government's own proposal. He said the government felt that what resulted from the working of the law was unfair.
