Under the provisions of the Income War Tax Act, if a taxpayer is dissatisfied with his assessment, within thirty days he serves notice of appeal directed to the Minister of National Revenue. That is not just the ordinary notice of appeal that one visualizes in connection with court proceedings. It is not only a notice of appeal; it is a statement of fact, and one has to incorporate with that the grounds of his appeal. In other words, it is equivalent to a factum on appeal, in the appeal courts of this country.
I am not objecting to that very much, because while it may have to be done rather hurriedly, there is a provision for a subsequent and fuller statement of facts and other grounds which may be submitted at a later stage. What I object to is that the notice of appeal, under the procedure laid down in the statute, is from Caesar to Caesar. It is not in accordance with the principles of British justice.
Here we have an assessment made by a Minister of National Revenue. That, of course, is notice to a taxpayer as to his position with respect to his income tax return as filed. Unless he takes action, of course that automatically goes into effect, and he is bound by the terms of the assessment. Should he be aggrieved, either on a point of fact or on a point of law, it is his inalienable right, under every principle of British justice, that he should have an appeal. The statute recognizes the principle, but sets out what I consider to be a non-British system of appeal. You appeal to the man who was your judge in the first instance, and you appeal on the same set of facts. Unless there has been a clear omission on the part of the taxing authority in the first instance, you appeal to the same taxing officer who previously assessed and judged. That is not an appeal at all. If it ended there it would be disastrous. As far as I understand, there is no opportunity to argue the appeal before the appellate court, if you can so call it; that is the minister. You are judged on the ' statement of facts and the grounds for appeal which you file in writing. As I said before, it is an appeal from Caesar to Caesar. That is bad in principle. If I have adequately stated the principle for which I am contending, I am sure the membership of this committee will agree with me.
I object that you are appealing to the tribunal which has already judged you, which has already imposed an assessment upon you.
It is not an appeal except in name. It is not even another trial, because there is no opportunity, except in the written submission that has to be made rather hurriedly, to argue your case on appeal. I say that to have that kind of appeal is a travesty on justice.

Fortunately the administration of the day provided an additional system. When the minister gives his second decision, which he does ex parte, and' refuses the appeal-I assume that is done in 99-9/10 per cent of the cases- there is a provision that the appellant may file notice of dissatisfaction and ask that the case be set down for hearing before the exchequer court. I should like to know just how many appeals the minister has allowed.
I am going to give the minister a constructive suggestion. I have already intimated that I do not consider this to be an appeal at all. The appeal ought to be to a judicial body of some kind. I have discussed this matter with more than one person and have come to the conclusion that the appeal should not be to the Minister of National Revenue. He has already judged the case on the same material. The appeal should 'be to an independent body, judicial in character, which would have the right to hear the parties to the appeal, including the crown. 'In my view this body should consist of a judge of a high court with the necessary character and ability and capacity. He should be surrounded with what in shipping law we would call nautical assessors; that is, he would have one or more chartered accountants, men who were versed' in>
income tax law and who understood the principle of the income tax structure.
The appeal would be to a body which would be receiving de novo the proposals of the appellant and viewing them dispassionately in the calm light of the facts and the law applicable thereto, and in accordance with the allegations set out in the factum filed by the appellant. Of course consideration would also be given to the right of the crown to reply in writing and to have the matter argued. That is the only way by which I can see that we would have a proper appeal. To-day the position is really a travesty on justice. It may be that that is too strong a term- to use. There 'is no personal reflection on the minister, as he will understand, and if he objects to the term I will withdraw it. But to me it is not an appeal at all. It is not fair to the subject whose rights are in question. It is a loaded court. A decision has already been reached on the same set of facts that will be before the appellate jurisdiction. I think all I have to do is to state the facts and this committee will agree that we ought to set up a new jurisdiction this session to hear these appeals. I believe that if the minister will consult with his officials in the income tax division he will find that there is a volume of opinion there to support the position which I take.
I do not see how the provision can be defended. I cannot recall having discussed
this matter in parliament before when the provisions were put there. If I were in the house and did not do so, I would say that I was recreant in my duty as a member of this house in allowing that sort of thing to go on the statute books. The only parallel I can find is in the customs department. In days gone by I used to have a considerable experience in connection with customs assessments and what-not, and I would appeal from the decision of the commissioner of customs to the minister of customs. I can remember only one case in a long line of cases that I handled before becoming a member of this house where the minister of customs reversed the decision of the commissioner of customs; I was successful only once in a series of cases.
You have to have such an overwhelmingly strong case that it would be a denial of justice to do otherwise than to grant the appeal. That is the only parallel I can find in the laws of Canada. I am not suggesting that the minister does not give some consideration to these appeals, but I wonder just how much consideration he does give. Does he sit down calmly with his advisers in a judicial atmosphere and consider the merits of these appeals? I am going to ask the Minister of National Revenue to tell us how many appeals have come before him since he has been minister of that department. I am going to go farther than that and ask him how many appeals have come before the department since this procedure was placed on the statute books and how many have been allowed.
Why is it that the appellant has not the right to be heard? To me the very essence of an appeal is the privilege that goes with it for the appellant or his counsel to state his case and argue it, as he would before a court of justice. Otherwise it is just going through the motions and form of an appeal. I suggest that in a democratic coufitry like Canada that is not good enough. I hope I have not overstated this case because I do not want to do anything like that. I am arguing now for the revision of the procedure relating to appeals.
Let us have a real appeal from the decision of the minister. The only analogy I would draw is an appeal from the judgment of a trial court. To appeal to the judge of a trial court against his own decision would be to me just so much futility. Let us have a real appeal, and I suggest a method which commends itself to my judgment.
There may be other methods that are perhaps better. Why should there not be an appeal direct, we will say, to the exchequer court of this country from the original assess-

Income War Tax
ment? It is not easy to make an appeal. You have first to put up security for costs in the sum of $400. That will prevent frivolous appeals. I suggest that that is a substantial sum to put up for security for costs in an appeal. In the ordinary appeals in my part of the country from the judgment of the trial court of king's bench to the court of appeal you do not have to put up any security for costs. I realize that if there were not something in the nature of security demanded there might be all kinds of frivolous appeals in the hope that perhaps some of them would stick and the appellant might win. They would incur no risk, and it would cost them only their out-of-pocket expenses. But here you have to put up $400 as security for costs when you give your notice of dissatisfaction with the assessment after the minister has formed his own judgment. That is a substantial sum. It certainly prevents frivolous appeals.
I do beg the minister to give consideration now, at this session of parliament, to reforming the law-and reform is long overdue- so that there shall be an appeal that will be in fact an appeal, to the end that justice may at least have a chance to function. I do not want the minister to take any wrong interpretation from that statement. He is a lawyer, and those of us who belong to the legal profession know that you cannot have a real appeal to a man who has already decided the matters at issue. What kind of appeal is that? It is just a pro forma appeal. It is not an appeal in fact at all or in essence. We ought to have something better than that in this country.

I cannot, of course, speak for the Minister of Finance, but I will bring to his attention the discussion which has arisen this evening. I thank

There is nothing that is causing the soldiers overseas more worry and trouble, and their families at home as well, than the principle involved in the assessment and the notification of assessments as well as appeal to the minister. We have two ministers in charge of this bill to-night-the parliamentary assistant and the Minister of National Revenue, both distinguished soldiers. I was in hopes that now we have reached1 the end of the fifth year of the war there might be some more just and equitable way of dealing with this matter and sometimes at the base from the point of view of the men serving overseas. In the first place, the relatives at home get the assessment and they do not know what to do with it. A good many of them have come and asked me what they should do with it. This section does not go far enough, or in my opinion it should be struck out altogether. The municipalities have a different way of approaching the principle of assessment and appeal contained in this 
system so far as the soldier overseas is concerned. When it comes to the men fighting in Italy and in France, and in the invasion, under the circumstances that obtain now, how will you reach the soldiers by notice of assessment? The municipalities do not sell property or real estate in arrears of taxes for anything less than three years arrears of taxes. The larger municipalities, in fact nearly all the municipalities, have some provision, and in some provinces through provincial legislation in regard to the taxation of men overseas and the penalties imposed upon them. The principle of the assessment is an important matter, and the soldier whose income is less than $4,000 should in my opinion be exempt for the period of the war. We should have a more modern system of assessment for civilians and soldiers alike, and you would get as much money out of the taxpayers as you do now. We have an excellent commissioner, a man who is unexcelled anywhere, but he and his staff are given an impossible task to perform, under the provisions of this bill.
I object to the last four or five words of the section extending the time of notice. The last words give the minister power to make the extension and these words should not appear in a revenue bill. The executive should not be given power to make rules and regulations. It is the duty of the House of Commons to examine revenue and all other control bills, ' every line of them, especially when they take these matters out of the control of parliament and vest them in the executive power. The same thing appears in every piece of legislation that has been presented to the house in war time; powers of this sort are left to the executive. That in my opinion is most objectionable. I do not see why we do not abolish this whole method of taxation and adopt the old income tax methods of the municipalities. Take a man with a small amount, say $4,000. Why not tax him 5, 10, 15 or 20 per cent, or what, is for war necessary on a percentage of the net income. In my opinion this whole system is wrong. This tax system is too long. The creation of the world is written in less than 600 words, and the Lord's Prayer is contained in sixty words, but here we have this long bill amended year after year. I do not blame the officials. Parliament is to blame for the present complex act and system. In my opinion we should adopt the old principle we had years ago. If a man has an income of two or three or four thousand dollars you should put an aggregate tax of 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25 per cent, or what is needed, on him. You have to get the money in any event for war purposes, and about fifty-five per cent of the revenue is being obtained through the income tax.

There should be a more reasonable method of assessment for men overseas because it worries the life out of them and their wives and relatives at home. Moreover, a lot of these men cannot pay. Where is a soldier to get money to pay as herein for taxes in arrears starting in 1939, all through 1940, 1941, 1942, 1943 and up to the present time? Where will the soldier get the money even, if he does get the assessment? It is going to be mailed to him overseas, but they do not get all the letters sent them by their families. I know the ministers and officials have laboured long and hard on this subject and know more about it than I do, but I have seen the application of some of these rules and regulations, and if lawyers at home cannot advise their clients how to make up their assessment, how will the soldiers in the invasion, with no one to help them, manage? There should be a stay for a year after the war so far as soldiers are concerned, to give them time to pay up arrears of taxes. A great many of them do not want to be in arrears because they will have to pay that money some time or another, but there should be some reduction in the rates charged men serving overseas, as compared with those who are not in the service. There should be some allowance in that connection, and a revision should be made all along the line. You could not have a simpler system of assessment than the old system we had years ago. There used to be three systems of taxation, federal, provincial and municipal, and I suggest that we should go back to the old method. Soldiers should not be worried in this way. The hon. member for
York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) invited others in the house, who have some experience in the matter of appeals to the minister, to express themselves in this connection. I think the hon. gentleman has performed a service in bringing this matter before the committee, just as he did yesterday when he brought another matter to its attention. I have had some experience in the matter of appeals to the minister, and I may say to the hon. member for York-Sunbury and to my other fellow members that my experience has been entirely happy and satisfactory. I have taken as many
as four appeals to the present minister in a single day, where the clients all lined up outside the door and one after another was heard. And in every case, although they were not successful, the clients went away feeling that they had had a fair deal; that their case had been heard and judicially handled and decided quite satisfactorily. At the same time I am of opinion that the system is not satisfactory.
I do not suggest that we should abolish the appeal to the minister. For those who wish to take it, it is all right, but there are others who do not wish to take it. I think we should have some system of judicial decisions that is separated entirely from the administration of the department. No minister responsible for the administration of his department can entirely separate himself-he may do it in his own mind, but it is in his own mind only- from the conditions under which he approaches the question.
There is some talk of an appeal to the exchequer court. That is all right. There is only one official in the exchequer court who would be acting. There might be more than one judge in the court, but only one would be engaged and the expenses do not need to be great. I have no sympathy with this business of charging a litigant 8400 as security for costs as is done in the Supreme Court of Ontario in certain circumstances. I have no sympathy with that at all. The public has an interest in this matter and it is the duty of the crown to decide questions of this kind. The officials should not be so taxed with business that they cannot attend to the matter of appeals of this kind. I do not see any reason for charging a man $400 security for costs in order to have some dispute between himself and the department adjudicated by some judicial official. As far as costs are concerned, we can argue that in every infringement of the criminal law; and yet we set up officials all over this province, scores of them, in Canada hundreds of them, who hear disputes between the subject and the crown, usually the issue being as to whether the individual is guilty. We do that with small costs, and we never think of charging costs or security for costs against anybody who appeals to a police magistrate for a mere decision. We ought to be able to have a judicial authority to whom the minister can refer questions which he does not himself wish to decide or to whom those who have questions which they do not care to leave to the minister may appeal. Expense would be slight; the principle would be good. I am satisfied the work-out would be satisfactory, and I support the idea of a judicial appeal in addition to the appeal to the minister.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury has brought up a very important point to-night, and I think he has put the situation clearly before the committee. He was, of course, dealing with the customary type of appeal; but since this war began there have been hundreds of thousands of Canadians paying income tax for the first time; many, many more people are affected by the income tax to-day than there were before the war, and very seriously affected. Has any consideration been given to providing some sort of appeal for the small businessman or for the individual who perhaps is not taxed a great deal, looking ,at it against the background of our billion dollar budgets, but from his point of view it does look large? He is simply out of luck. He does not have this appeal, for he cannot raise $400 and pay his owp lawyer besides. It is an impossible situation for him. I mentioned it when I was speaking in the budget debate last week. I have had representations from men who feel that they have been unfairly treated in their assessments; they go before the assessor and complain and sometimes they are treated in a rather cavalier fashion. In the course of my speech I quoted from a letter from one of those small businessmen; he pointed out there were those who felt that they were getting a raw deal in some cases and yet could do nothing about it. He put it in this way:
And yet, after a short time, they paid the assessments so that they could get the worry off their minds and get on with their business, knowing well the difficulties and costs of appeal.
That statement shows a very unfortunate situation with regard to our Income War Tax Act. It is a very important act. It is an important act not only for the years of the war but also for far into the post-war years. The Canadian people should feel that they are being fairly treated under it. If they get what they consider a raw deal, then' they should have some proper method of appealing. I suggested that consideration be given to providing for a cheap and summary appeal where smaller amounts are involved; it might be to a county court judge, or perhaps to a judge of a superior court. Has any consideration been given to setting up some appeal court, making some arrangements for an appeal of that type?

Why would it not be possible to provide a summary appeal, a cheap appeal that could be heard out in the districts? It is all right where a person lives in Montreal, and has to come to Ottawa to argue an appeal; but it is an entirely different matter when one has to come from Vancouver or Halifax. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the main reason is the desirability, at any rate, and probably the necessity of having some uniformity in decisions in these matters. I do not know of any advanced country where the ordinary county court, shall we say, or district court, hears these tax appeals. I know that is not so in England or in the United States. I do not know of any country where appeals of this kind are left to the lower courts. They are almost invariably decided either by special courts set up in the first instance, or by a high court. Here we have the exchequer court.

Could there be a taxation
appeal board which would sit in different parts of the country? What would be the objection to that?

speechtext: And they would move across the country?

speechtext: That was suggested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury this evening, namely, that a special appeal tribunal be set up to hear tax appeals.

Some consideration ought to be given to geographical situation. It is all right in a big case to have counsel come to Ottawa to present their arguments. But I can imagine cases, minor in amounts, where it would be cheaper to pay than to proceed, if one had to come to Ottawa.
However, I did not rise to argue that point; I shall leave that to my hon. friend. One interesting point has been disclosed by this discussion to-night for the first time, namely, that appellants would have the right to, go before the minister, after having filed notice of appeal. That is news to me. I did not know it was the practice or the custom, or that that courtesy was extended to an appellant. Certainly there is nothing in the statute to provide for that.. It must be a matter of courtesy.
Of course, I can understand coming before the deputy minister, arguing out the matter informally, and trying to convince him that you are right. But I do not consider that an appeal. That is just a sort of preliminary interrogatory. Usually it is done in a very different manner, off the record, and usually one comes away just the same as when he started. If it is the custom of the minister to hear counsel, or to hear parties without counsel, then I think the public ought to know about it. I would suggest to the minister that if that became widely known he would be swamped. He had better not encourage it, because I can see where his time would be taken up completely by that sort of thing.
What I am arguing for is to get away from the .administrative atmosphere once the assessment is made. Then the function of the department is exhausted, the minister is functus officio, and the matter ought to go to some outside tribunal. I hope consideration will be given to the suggestion made to-day, and that something substantial will be done before the bill founded upon these resolutions is passed. I shall not labour the point further, because the position has been made clear.

There is no secret about the procedure. It is necessary to file formal notice of appeal, lest your rights go by the board. That is particularly so in connection

But I think the observations made by the hon. member who has just spoken and by the minister wth respect to research, on the part of both the government and industry, would generally commend themselves to hon. members. I live in a section which is highly industrialized, one which competes very closely with a great city having industry on a large scale, and just on the opposite side of the river. There tremendous research enterprises are undertaken, and to an amazing degree. If hon. members ever have an oportunity of visiting the General Motors Corporation in Detroit, for instance, and look through their research laboratory, they will be amazed. I doubt if any university in this country has anything to compare with those laboratories.
We have to compete, and1 will have to compete with that sort of thing. One must recognize, then, the great need for research in our own plants. I have seen many of our graduates from our universities forced to go across the river and to take jobs over there because there were no adequate opportunities in these lines for them in Canada. If we can encourage industry, and particularly industry where there would be opportunities to engage in research, and to hire many of the products of our own universities, nothing but profit can ensue.
The national research council has been supported by the hon, member for Cape Breton South, and quite properly so. My main purpose in rising, however, was to suggest this, that not only is there an opportunity for industry itself in this provision, but there will be an opportunity in another direction, because the resolution provides that-
. . . expenditures in respect of scientific research directly or indirectly related to the taxpayer's business . . .
-are to be made deductible. This affords to industry an opportunity to do something which industry in this country has not done, and that is an opportunity to assist in scholarship endowments and, through direct financial grants, to assist the research work of our universities.
There are in this country universities which are carrying on research of tremendous value to industry in Canada, but which receive no assistance whatsoever from industry. I have one large industry in mind which was approached within the last six months by a university in connection with a grant to cover a certain scheme of research. It was a type of research from which the industry in question had profited for a period of eight years.
Under this resolution many of our universities, none of which is over-heavily endowed to conduct studies of this kind, would be afforded an opportunity. I have received a communication recently from Dalhousie university, through the social science and labour school established there. Here an opportunity was afforded individuals who wanted to assist in the development of social science research. The labour school is something that would commend itself to anyone interested in labour.
Income War Tax

However, the department took the view that contributions made by individuals to assist in these efforts were not deductible.
I hope the minister will find it possible under resolution 23 to permit contributions by individuals, companies or otherwise, in connection with the prosecution of the kind of thing concerning which I have spoken, and as it applies to Dalhousie university. I should hope this might properly come under the resolution now before us. I trust the commissioner who has this matter in hand will bear in mind what I have said, and that in interpreting resolution 23 he will afford Dalhousie university in the setting up of its labour school something which I think it deserves by way of encouragement.
Will this be available to farmers? Will farming be considered a business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
There is no limitation suggested by the department with regard to the amount which any person can deduct in this manner?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Consideration will be given in the bill to providing safeguards and restrictions. I do not know just how far we should go. In Great Britain one of the reasons given by the chancellor of the exchequer for making a similar provision, going at least as far as this, was that he wanted to provide for buoyancy of revenue in the future. It is by no means a total loss of revenue when you engage in industrial research. You are casting your bread upon the waters.
I agree with that.

As I pointed out to the minister, I am not going to argue this at all because I do not know enough about this. Our research laboratories have been practically at a standstill since the outbreak of the war in so far as research into peace-time requirements are concerned. They are doing a wonderful job on war -work for national defence, the army, the navy, the air force and munitions and supply. They are handling practically everything in that field that they are asked to do. But their staff is small, and attention should be focused on the necessity of staffing our research laboratories and getting ready for peace-time requirements.
When a private company develops anything new it may be put on the market, but it is sold at a price at which ninety-eight per cent of the people of this country cannot buy it. When anything is turned out by a private company it is sold at a price which does not

permit the great majority of the people to benefit. I have worked in one industry for thirty years, and what research have they carried on? What improvements have they made? None.
It would have been better if they had.

It would have been better if they had. They are carrying on a little research now at the Sydney steel plant. The federal Department of Agriculture has an appropriation for the development of a fertilizer and the provincial government is assisting. However, I noticed the other day that one of the provincial men who is working with them had to spend three or four days with our national research people getting the necessary information and polishing up on the thing in order that it might be completed. In the final analysis the real work is being done here.
I do not see any solution of the future of this country in research. No doubt a lot of it has to be done. We are in an age where we are in the hands of the scientists. But if these things are to be developed in such a way that they will not be available to the majority of the people, we shall be wasting our time. I do not think the people of Canada- realize the extent of our research facilities in Ottawa, and they should be extended and expanded so that we could make these things available to the people.
TTiese private companies tie up the patents after they develop these things. They would not release the method of processing fuel. A senate committee in Washington is trying to break the monopoly of the oil companies in this connection. This research was done many years ago, but the patents are held internationally by the oil companies and will not be used until those companies are ready to make them available. I have no intention of delaying the minister any longer, but I just wanted to make that one point. These-things should be made available to the people in order that they can use them, but if you depend upon private industry they will lock them away in their vaults until they are ready to release them.

With the consent of the committee I should like to revert to resolution 20, which reads:
That the right of the minister to reassess or make additional assessments in respect of any tax year be limited to a period of six years from the date of the original assessment.
I wonder if the minister would consent to making that six years from the date of filing the original return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, no, I do not think so.

Income War Tax

It is a long period, 6ix years of uncertainty. I think it is a condemnation of the department if the minister does not accept the situation. I had occasion to look at a company circular recently, and I think the return had not been returned or the assessment made final by the department going back to 1938 or 1939. After five or six years they may finally get the assessment from the department, and then there will be another six years during which the assessment can be considered and before it is made final. That would make a total of ten to twelve years. Surely six years after the filing of the return should be adequate for the department to make any necessary check-up, subject always, of course, to any fraud or the other reservations in the section. Otherwise I think it stands as a shocking condemnation of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My first reaction is not favourable, but the hon. gentleman may think that is temperamental. This is a problem for the Department of National Revenue rather than for the Department of Finance.

The resolution is brought forward for one particular reason, to give some certainty to business. I am pointing out that there is tire possibility of defeating the whole purpose. In the case I have mentioned, they are already six or seven years behind and now they want an additional six years before the assessment will be considered as being final. The department need never give an original assessment unless they see fit. This is one of the outstanding matters of administration in connection with our act and one of the cases where there is, shall I call it a loophole against the taxpayer and in favour of the government. This does not occur in the British and United States acts. We have never had a limitation in our act and now it is proposed -to make it six years from the date of the original assessment. The Minister of National Revenue has stated that his department is not so far behind, and if he is correct then there should be no harm in saying that the tax return shall be final six years after filing, and not after the date of the original assessment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can think of cases, perhaps not numerous, where litigation has extended over several years and you could not make a ne,w assessment. However, I do not think that is the main argument against the hon. gentleman's submission. At the present time there is no limitation; the Department of National Revenue could go back to the beginning of the Income War Tax Act and make
assessments if facts came to light which showed that a tax was payable. We are taking a long step in advance when we put a limitation on.
You are catching up with other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be. But we are taking a step in advance and I think we had better go a little slowly about this. We had better try the six years at any rate, and then if we can get the assessing machinery which can function very promptly, possibly the time could be counted from the date of the return. But we have not that, machinery at the present time. It is impossible to get the staff and it is impossible to make the assessment with great promptness.

There has not been much pressure brought upon the Department of National Revenue because the same delay was in existence before the war. Then we had unemployment and accountants were seeking jobs. There is now the excuse that you cannot get additional accountants. Evidently there has been no pressure on the department up to date and it is high time that it should not longer be administered like a country grocery store.

That the minister may allow depreciation at double the rates normally allowed in respect of .bona fide new investments made after a date to be declared by the governor in council; and. in such event, the .taxpayer will be required to charge in any subsequent year at least one-half the rates normally allowed: Provided, however, in the case of a sale of assets in respect of which special depreciation has been so allowed, the minister may revise the assessments of the vendor for the years when the special depreciation was allowed, by disallowing as a deduction a pro rata portion of the special depreciation allowed, to the extent of the excess of the selling price over the depreciated cost of the sand assets, less the amount of the depreciation normally allowed on the said assets, and less the excess, if any, of the selling price over the undepreciated cost of the said assets: Provided further that the portion of any loss attributable to the allowance of special depreciation shall not constitute a loss for purposes of resolution number twenty-two.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As explained in the budget speech, the general purpose of this proposal for depreciation up to double the ordinary rates is to allow companies to proceed with planning for post-war expansion or conversion of existing plant to peace-time needs. It is impossible for the government to state at this time when the excess profits tax will be removed, but this feature will enable the income from peace-time projects to be applied
Income War Tax

against the cost of making the new investments at a time when the excess profits tax may still be in force. This, of course, does not mean that the profits from such new investment will escape taxation. It merely means that depreciation charges which are a proper charge against profits before tax may be taken at an accelerated rate from the beginning of such investment.
The measure is safeguarded by requiring an adjustment in profit and loss account in the event of subsequent sale of the assets in respect of which speedy depreciation has been allowed. Furthermore, any loss shown in profits and loss account as the result of this depreciation in excess of normal rates shall not be carried backward or forward as provided in resolution 22. A company is not compelled to take the double rates, although it must take at least half the normal rate allowed.
A similar provision exists with respect to accelerated depreciation granted by the war contracts depreciation board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The minister always has the power of revising his assessment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The point I am making is 'that if accelerated depreciation is approved by the minister, there is a provision that if the assets depreciated are sold, and sold before they would have been fully depreciated under the ordinary basis, then a portion of the special depreciation which has been granted is taken back into profits.
What is the full import of that clause in regard to subsequent years, that it must take at least half the ordinary depreciation? I do not understand just what bearing that has.	*

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

They must take half the
rates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I shall not discuss the resolution at the length at which it might be discussed. As the minister and his assistant realize, it touches very closely the basic issue between the economic philosophy represented by the party to which my hon. friends opposite belong and the economic philosophy of this group. During the course of my speech on the budget debate I joined with others in offering certain congratulations to the Minister of Finance. I believe that he was not in his place, at the time so that I might repeat one of the things on which I congratulated him quite sincerely, and that was the clarity with which I feel he states his position so far as his economic philosophy is concerned and as regards what he feels should be the postwar policy of this country. He made it clear during the debate on the budget and in the debate on the second reading of the Bank Act that he feels that post-war Canada should be founded on the principle of strengthening private enterprise. It is an old idea-at least that is the way we characterize it-that if assistance is given to private enterprise, somehow or another the benefits of that assistance will filter down through to the community as a whole. The position we take is that that system has been tried and found wanting, and that the time has come, particularly in view of some of the experiences which this government and other governments have had during this war, to turn to the principle of wider public control of industry and of our economic life.	_ _
Further, I want to congratulate the minister on his consistency in this respect. From the position that he takes, this resolution represents a perfectly logical course to pursue. It is, as the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, very similar to the course that has been pursued during the war in the granting of huge amounts for special depreciation to certain firms about which we have spoken in this house from time to time.
I rise at this point only to say that we in this group feel that the country is taking a backward step if it is still held that we can depend on private enterprise or that assistance of this land can give us progress in the postwar world. I hope that the day will come when we shall have a government that will follow a different policy.
The minister when he referred to these resolutions in his budget speech on June 26 said that this provision would permit private industry to transfer some of its income from a period when war-time tax rates may still be in effect to a later period when the taxpayer may expect normal taxation. In other words, I think the minister will agree that it is correct to say that private industry is being

Income War Tax
given a chance to gamble on lower tax rates at a later period. That gamble has to be within certain limits, in that the depreciation may not be greater than double the normal rates nor can it be less than half the normal rates. But within those limits private industry is given this chance to gamble that tax rates are much higher now than they will be later on, and to say, "therefore let us get as much depreciation now as we can, while the tax rates in effect are quite high." I confess that from the minister's viewpoint that is at least consistent; it is a consistent way of encouraging private enterprise to try to build this new Canada which we hope will come after the war. My contention is that private industry has been tried and found wanting, and that, consistent though this may be with the minister's philosophy, it will not do the job which needs to be done in the post-war period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to undertake now to reply to the hon. gentleman. He has, I think, made a fair statement of the issue. We are doing this to encourage investment by private enterprise; that is right, and we think the country will need it. He thinks the investment should be made by government, I presume, or some agency other than private enterprise.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Substantially that is so

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will not pursue that. But his leader made a speech on the budget to which I just want to refer. He said this, as reported in Hansard, at page 4351:
Here _ is another instance of the familiar subsidizing of private enterprises that cannot stand on their own feet. Its plain meaning, as I take it at least, is that the taxpayer is to put up one-half of the new investments but will get nothing in return.
That is as far from the truth as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The statement is incorrect, and I do not need to elaborate its meaning. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) who has just spoken knows the meaning of these matters pretty clearly, and I do not think he will contend that that statement is correct.

I might point out that the statement of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is entirely wrong, because he talks about these alleviations of hardship on business in some cases, and in other cases about certain incentives, as being something handed out to business. To me it has always been amazing that business has been able to stand the taxation put upon it, because business does not eat or consume the product which it has or it gets; it is simply an aggregation of people, who have got together
in the form of a cooperative, if you like, and have pooled their resources and created work for other people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Aluminium Limited.

Certainly if it had not been for United "States enterprise coming over here we would never have given twenty-five thousand Canadian workmen jobs, and as one of my colleagues on the committee said, all you could see was that there was a lot of water going to waste up there. No raw materials were taken out of Canada, but we have given twenty-five thousand men employment in doing a great job. One of the most wonderful contributions in the world has been made to the production of aluminum, and the water is still flowing down to the sea. It is a wonderful job which the Aluminum company has done. I do not think it would have been possible for either the Canadian government * or the people of Canada to have accomplished that great project without the assistance of this United States company. I may tell the hon. member that the company can produce in three days enough aluminum for Canada's requirements; the rest is all for export. What right would the people or the goverment of Canada have to go into that business under such conditions? However, I do not want to be drawn aside on that particular topic. We have talked about it before; we may talk about it at another time.
I wish to point out that business in this country is not left to itself; it is very heavily taxed; and in many cases there are-I will not call them penalties-exactions made upon business which make it almost impossible for business to go ahead. It was the purpose of this government, when war broke out, so to intensify taxation that it was impossible for any business dealing with civilian production to go ahead or expand. It was meant that these should be throttled, and they were throttled by the rate of taxation we have to-day. No measure could be more socialistic in peace times than a continuance of the taxation policy of the present government and I assume that it will not be continued. But I want to point out, contrary to what was said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the C.C.F., in his remarks on the budget, that these are not a hand-out to business; they are a certain measure of relief because business is very heavily taxed in this country. To my mind it is wrong to tax tools. Business is simply a tool, and you cannot have employees unless you have employers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I misunderstood the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Income War Tax

I did not understand he was contending that we were making a hand-out to business, but if he was so contending I would not have agreed that that is what we are doing.
That is not what he said, either.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No. The minister understood me correctly, but the hon. member for Rosedale did not quite get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the committee will permit me for just a minute, the hon. member for Rosedale is correct in saying that we have put on very heavy taxation; and we have certain rules about depreciation which may be regarded as normal rules applicable to business as a whole. In cases of new investments there is a relaxation of these rules to some extent. That is not a hand-out to business.
The attitude taken by the C.C.F. generally is that when you get heavy taxes on business, no matter how heavy they are you should keep them there; you should1 never relax. We are always criticized, I think, by the C.C.F. whenever we relax taxation on business, and that is consistent with the policy, as I understand it, of the C.C.F. party, because they regard it as in the public interest that burdens on private business cannot be too heavy because private business is old fashioned; the way to build a new country is to have an entirely different organization of business; therefore it is in the public interest to make the burdens very, very heavy, and it is always against the public interest to lighten those burdens in any way.
It is not making a hand-out to adjust your taxation to some extent in order to encourage the expansion of business, and I do not think the hon. gentleman accused us of trying to make a hand-out here. But that is what I understand to be the issue between us. I do not complain about the C.C.F. when they come along and say, as the leader of the C.C.F. did in his budget speech, that we should not lighten those burdens no matter how brutally heavy they are, that they should stay there; that these people should not be functioning in that way and that the heavier the burdens the better. That is the belief of my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party. It is not mine.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I want to say, despite
such disagreement as there may be between the minister and myself, that his understanding as to the issue between us is quite clear. But there is just this change in emphasis in whi he has said now by way of describing C.C.F. policy in this respect to which I should like to point. The minister spoke as though

our only interest so far as taxation of business is concerned is to impose upon it the heaviest possible burden. Now, so long as you have the system of private enterprise, capitalism, in effect as we have it to-day, we feel that the taxes should be sufficiently heavy to drain off to the community as a whole the wealth of the community which in the first instance is getting into private hands.

It does not get into
private hands. It is double taxation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That policy must be distinguished from the positive policy which we feel should be taken under the kind of government we ourselves advocate. In power, our concern would be, not with what the minister feels to be negative forms of taxation, but with positive means of developing the economy of this country and increasing production. The difference between the minister and me, between the Liberals and the C.C.F., is that he and his party feel that production can be encouraged and employment increased by assistance to private industry such as the minister consistently provides; whereas we feel that these things can best be accomplished by the government itself in the name of the people taking the initiative, somewhat after the pattern which has been followed during the course of this war.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: This is related to the resolution that I spoke on a while ago, resolution 24. I shall not take undue time, but I should like to make a brief statement and I will be concrete about it. also items of expenditure in Newfoundland and in British Guiana for the Demerara Bauxite Company Limited. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Then in turn they were permitted to deduct from their profits the total cost of this construction. I want to point out that this construction in British Guiana included some pretty extensive items, a great number of railroads and bridges, and the main item of course is the plant and equipment to produce 1,500,000 tons of bauxite per annum. Last year I checked on this matter in the library and found that that figure is more than three times the total annual production of bauxite in British Guiana before the war. In other words, through this means we have helped to make possible the building in British Guiana of a very extensive plant which is the entire property of Aluminium Limited, the parent company in Canada. Up to the present I take it the dividends on the operation of the Demerara Company which have come to Aluminium Limited have been taxable and yet, despite that arrangement Aluminium Limited has got along very well in the profits that it has been able to pile up year by year, and the dividends it has been able to pay. Entirely apart from any argument there may be between us as to the theory behind it, I cannot see the necessity

Rules oj the House
for granting relief on this point to a company such as this, particularly in view of the kind of assistance it has received. I say that recognizing the difference there is between us as to the definition of that word. I see that the Minister of Mines and Resources is interested in this. He and I had some arguments about this very subject last year relating to the question as to what the Canadian government eould do about the bauxite company since it was outside Canada. I now call to his attention the fact that it is wholly owned in Canada by a Canadian company and that these extensive developments were financed by this arrangement that we have detailed several times.
My point is that with all that assistance, with the arrangements that we have behind it, I feel that it is going a little bit too far to add to that this further relief from taxation, which, apart from whatever theoretical differences there may be between us, apparently is not necessary because of the profits that Aluminium Limited has been able to show on the old basis.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Only relief from what in effect is triple taxation. This is not relief to shareholders of Aluminium Limited from taxation.
Progress reported.
